book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth

chapters.relation: The editor's introduction surveys the sprawling Frankenstein pop-culture corpus the book will dissect - Whale's 1931 'It's Alive!' scene, the lovable Herman Munster, Mel Brooks's Young Frankenstein, Dean Koontz's Dr. Helios, Boris Karloff's grunting brute, and I, Frankenstein's Adam - insisting the creature now lives in hundreds of films, shows, and novels rather than Shelley's text alone. It frames the book's guiding shocks: whether a re-animated corpse-man has a soul, whether making monsters differs from making babies, and whether Frankenstein's maligned creation would be right to seek to end all of us. It closes by inviting readers to peer into the monster's dull yellow eyes with the lights left on and the door barred.

Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.

Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.

Jacquette treats Frankenstein as the modern myth of scientific overreach whose two-century grip on pop culture (over a thousand films, Frankenberry cereal) rests on three stitched-together ingredients: Enlightenment faith in applied science, the mortality-awareness of the logician's 'All men are mortal,' and Prometheus-style retribution for challenging nature - while insisting Shelley's tale is science fiction, not supernatural. Victor's real crime is not daring science but abandoning his nameless creation to raise itself, so that 'if he had taken appropriate care of the monster he made, he might not have made such a monster.' The chapter closes with Wittgenstein's remark (Philosophical Investigations §261) that philosophy ends in the wish to 'emit an inarticulate sound,' matched to the Creature's ultimate question 'What was I?' answered only with groans, as Igor's hunting horn fades over the credits of Young Frankenstein.

Casetta and Tambolo dissect the 'Frankenfood' metaphor: metaphors map a familiar source domain (the Monster) onto a poorly known target (genetically modified organisms, like the 'Frankenfish' salmon), but the mapping fails because the Monster is a genetically heterogeneous chimera assembled from dead bodies while the engineered salmon is a genetically homogeneous hybrid grown from a single fertilized egg. Framing the question with Aristotle's view of metaphysics as the study of what things ultimately are, and applying Kripke-style origin essentialism and natural-kind essentialism, they show that being a patchwork is no essential property at all - our own symbiotic bacteria outnumber our 'human' cells - so Monster and GMO are not entities of the same kind. The metaphor should be discarded as intellectual junk, yet its allure persists because the living corpse-patchwork disturbs our fantasy of ourselves as pure, unmixed organisms.

Kokotz casts Victor as a pioneer of human 'enhancement' whose eight-foot daemon - stronger, faster, smarter, kinder, and vegetarian - actually achieved his goal of perfecting the human body, yet whose hideous appearance locked him out of society and love, twisting success into catastrophe: the 'Midas problem' of getting exactly what you wished for. Victor's deeper error was trusting Mill's On Liberty test that what people actually desire is thereby desirable; desires come from the human mind rather than nature, so a desired enhancement can make things worse, as the daemon's revenge on William, Henry, and Elizabeth proves. The lesson is institutional as well as conceptual: science must not proceed behind closed doors but under shared ethical oversight, since a Frankensteinian breakthrough carries too much responsibility for any single scientist to bear.

Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'

Fitzpatrick runs Marx's account of alienated labor from the 1844 Manuscripts through the novel: Victor's creature is the product of estranged labor, 'an alien object exercising power over him,' which he cannot name, comes to loathe, and which finally destroys him - the devaluation of the creator tracking the increasing value of the thing made, while workers become commodities producing commodities. The De Laceys' eviction in Branagh's Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and the Ingolstadt cholera riots stage class struggle at feudalism's end, and Victor's failure to self-actualize (to 'hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon... criticize after dinner') shows how capitalism turns science into 'a tool of our own destruction.' The chapter closes with 'Frankenstorm' climate change as the alienated externality par excellence - capitalists selling us the rope with which we hang ourselves.

Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.

Pötzsch explains the monster through Rousseau's Émile: innately good ('Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature'), the creature is corrupted because he experienced civilization 'too much and too soon' - the exact inverse of Rousseau's negative education, which shields the heart from vice instead of commanding, and lets the child learn 'through the mere force of things.' Victor knew his parents' model of paternal duty ('a deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life') yet abandoned his offspring and refused the female companion Rousseau deems essential to social development, so that wickedness born of weakness ('if I cannot inspire love, I will cause fear') murders William, Clerval, and Elizabeth. Shelley, a Rousseau admirer, makes Victor's science - an attempt to conquer rather than follow nature, fed by competitive professors at Ingolstadt - the very thing that dooms his parenting.

King weighs whether Victor or his creation bears the blame, opening with a thought experiment in which a neighbor's self-aware android burns your town and asking 'does he deserve to share that fate?' Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.

Galliott treats Frankenstein as the template for blaming lethal autonomous robots: Victor alone created his creature, but today's 'frankennovation' - Ronald Arkin's 'ethical governor' algorithms, DARPA funding, degree programs in robot warfare, and the South African robotic cannon that killed nine spectators - distributes responsibility across engineers, educators (Victor's father and Professors Krempe and Waldman, who never properly warned him about Agrippa's 'sad trash'), universities, and the military-industrial complex. Yet Shelley's articulate, Paradise Lost-quoting monster is a rational, intentional killer who can be held morally responsible and even punished, as Rob Sparrow demands of machines. Because responsibility does not dilute with numbers - two murderers do not get half a life sentence each - the chapter concludes that everyone in the chain, and all of us who do nothing to stop it, shares the blame for monstrous creations.

Hess asks whether the monster has a soul and makes him the test case between physicalism (Kim, Churchland, van Inwagen) and dualism: recasting Frank Jackson's Mary as a color-blind monster who learns every physical fact about color vision, receives new eyes on Walton's ship, and then learns the 'what it is like' of seeing red for the first time, he argues there are nonphysical mental facts, so physicalism is false. He then runs Plantinga's argument that we are not our bodies or brains through a machine that replaces the monster's parts and hemispheres one by one while he stays conscious, and adds near-death out-of-body evidence like Maria's window-ledge shoe to suggest we can exist disembodied. The upshot is symmetric: whatever we conclude about the monster's soul we must conclude about our own - so be careful about assuming who does and does not have a soul, even monsters.

Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement holding that we should use technology to overcome aging and death and transcend current human limits (de Grey, Max More, Bostrom, Harris).
holes.why: Chapter 10 stages its whole debate about radical life extension between Shelley's warning and transhumanists who call death the greatest of all evils, but the taxonomy has no transhumanism slug.

holes.name: Liberal Eugenics
holes.what: The program of using genetic and reproductive technologies for parent-consumer-chosen human enhancement, which Habermas (The Future of Human Nature) argues undermines moral equality and autonomy by turning creation into manufacture.
holes.why: Chapter 11's core argument applies Habermas's critique of liberal eugenics to Venter's synthetic life and Victor's creation, and no existing slug names the doctrine.

holes.name: Scientism (unlimited faith in science)
holes.what: The optimism that with enough time and resources science can control virtually every human adversity, including death itself.
holes.why: Chapter 13 identifies faith in unlimited scientific progress as the first of the three ingredients of the Frankenstein myth, and the taxonomy lacks any slug for it.

holes.name: Conceptual Metaphor (source and target domains)
holes.what: The theory that metaphors map a familiar source domain onto a less-known target domain and shape how we see the world (unidirectionality; scientific metaphors like 'selfish gene' or 'world as machine').
holes.why: Chapter 15's entire evaluation of the 'Frankenfood' metaphor is conducted in this framework, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.

holes.name: Human Enhancement
holes.what: Technologically improving human bodies and minds beyond medical treatment, up to conquering disease and death, by taking evolution into our own hands.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Victor as an enhancement pioneer and argues enhancement is not good in itself (the Midas problem); the generic applied-ethics slug does not name the concept.

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Basic Argument ('The Impossibility of Moral Responsibility') holds that no one can be morally responsible, since responsibility for actions would require responsibility for how one is, ad infinitum.
holes.why: Chapter 20's verdict that the monster is not responsible for his evil character rests on Strawson's impossibilism, and the taxonomy contains no Strawson.

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's theory that human motivation climbs from basic physiological and safety needs through the 'love need' to higher needs like prestige and self-actualization.
holes.why: Chapter 22 explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a deprived 'love need', making the hierarchy load-bearing for its analysis of who is to blame.

holes.name: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
holes.what: Jean Piaget's model of children's reasoning developing through the concrete operational (ages 7-11) and formal operational (adolescence onward) stages.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Piaget's stages to assess whether the monster had developed the mature reasoning needed for moral responsibility.

holes.name: Diffusion of Responsibility
holes.what: The tendency of people in a chain of responsibility to feel and act less responsibly because each assumes someone else will intervene ('I didn't do it').
holes.why: Chapter 23's conclusion about killer robots and monsters is that blame spreads across many hands without diluting, and diffusion of responsibility is the named risk no taxonomy slug captures.

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The view that humans are entirely physical beings with no immaterial parts such as souls, mental life being wholly a matter of brain states.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames the soul question as physicalism versus dualism, but the taxonomy offers only dualist slugs like cartesian-dualism.
